entries.note: Literally a description of the earth: geo- means earth, and -graphy means writing, recording or drawing.
Greek and Latin first used it for the ends of an axis, the one the night sky turns around; the magnetic sense came later.
Literally a glob; it only came to mean planet Earth around the mid-1500s, not long before the Globe Theatre was named.
Meant ground, like Latin terra, before it referred to the planet.
Named because it divides the earth into equal parts, the hemispheres.
From Greek tropos, 'to turn': at the solstice the sun appears to turn back; related to [[trope]] and [[zoetrope]].
Like [[tropic]], a 'turn'; Latin tropus meant a figure of speech, literally a turn of phrase, which gave the recurring storytelling trope.
An early spinning animation device, often showing a galloping horse; the name means a movement spin and is related to [[tropic]].
Its lines run north to south and are the long ones; Jess remembers it with the mnemonic 'long is tall, lat is fat', contrasting it with [[latitude]].
Contrasted with [[longitude]] in the mnemonic 'long is tall, lat is fat'; its lines get very short near the poles.
Literally the same as [[container]]: con- 'together' plus -tinent 'held', so continents are areas held together.
Unable to contain yourself, related to [[continent]]; it first meant unrestrained sexual desire and only later referred to the bowels.
From Latin contra, 'opposite you': the land you look out on and are faced with, so 'countryside' is the earlier sense.
From Dutch landschap, 'land-ship'; painters borrowed it for pictures of the countryside, so it named paintings before scenery. The ending is [[-ship]].
A suffix as in lordship and friendship, also found in [[landscape]]; it is related to [[shape]], means shaped like, and German has -schaft.
Contains [[deer]]: Old English wilde deor meant wild animals, and Middle English added -ness; it was later equated with [[desert]], meaning a place without people.
First meant any beast or animal and later narrowed to the specific animal, as seen in [[wilderness]].
From Old English heorot, a word for deer; Heorot is also the hall in Beowulf, named for stags because they were linked with royalty.
From an Old English word for deer, alongside the source of [[hart]].
A noun built on Greek bios, 'life': a place where life is.
A small [[biome]], such as the gut bacteria Rob thought of first.
Something that rises above the earth; related to [[mount]], [[mound]], [[eminent]], [[menace]], [[promontory]] and [[prominent]], which all share a sense of sticking out.
Related to [[mountain]] through the idea of sticking out; the hosts debate how to pronounce it.
The Germanic counterpart of Romance [[mountain]]; no fixed height separates the two, and the threshold varies by country and surrounding terrain.
From Latin forestis silva, 'outside woods': royal hunting grounds, not necessarily wooded; related to [[foreign]] and [[sylvan]], and contrasted with Germanic [[wood]].
A modern term from early-1900s ecology that became the preferred scientific name for the biome, contrasted with [[jungle]].
From Hindi for any wilderness or uncultivated land, from a Sanskrit word for arid terrain; English speakers applied it to dense forest.
A place without people, not a sandy place; from Latin deserere, to unjoin or forsake, which is related to [[series]].
An island that is deserted, not a sandy island as Rob had long assumed; see [[desert]].
Means desert, so 'Sahara Desert' is literally 'desert desert', a [[pleonasm]].
A redundant phrase like Sahara Desert; close to [[tautology]] but used more in linguistics, and pleonasms don't sound as wrong.
Close to [[pleonasm]] but also used in maths; tautologies like 'ATM machine' sound more obviously repetitive.
From an old Celtic word for river, so England's many Rivers Avon are 'river river'.
The Viking word for a river, so England's many Rivers Ouse are also redundant names.
From an Ojibwe term meaning great river, so 'Mississippi River' is 'great river river'.
Tahoe itself means lake, so the name is 'Lake Lake'.
Mauna means mountain, so 'Mount Mauna Kea' is redundant; measured from base to top, it's the world's tallest mountain.
From Spanish sabana, 'treeless plain', from Taíno zabana: a Caribbean word that Europeans later applied to the African biome.
From the Maa language of the Maasai, meaning endless plain.
Borrowed from Russian and, like [[savanna]], means treeless plain; we use the Russian word because steppes lie mostly around Russia.
The North American counterpart of [[savanna]] and [[steppe]]; the word is French because the French were there to name them.
Russian word for boreal forest, possibly of Turkic or Mongolic origin; it's the largest land biome, with needle-leaved conifers.
Means northern, as in [[Aurora Borealis]]; Borealis is a later Latin word, unlike classical [[septentriones]].
Basically means something squidgy; related to German [[Schwamm]], sponge or mushroom, and to [[sump]].
German for sponge or mushroom, related to [[swamp]]; TV make-up artists used a Schwämmchen, a little sponge, on Rob.
Related to [[swamp]]; used since the mid-1500s, first for a marsh, and for a pit that collects water from about 1650.
An Old English word for a wetland.
An Irish word for a wetland; in ecology, a rain-fed acidic wetland where peat forms and bog bodies stay preserved.
Another Old English word for a marsh.
An Old Norse word for a marsh.
The newest of these wetland words: an 18th-century compound of the much older 'wet' and 'land'.
From Latin riparia, 'riverbank', while flumen and amnis named the water itself, so a river is named for its bank; see [[riparian]].
Relates to rivers and streams, but in Latin originally to riverbanks; related to [[river]].
French for river, from the same Latin root as [[river]]; the hosts can't say how it differs from [[fleuve]], guessing one is bigger.
The other French word for river besides [[rivière]]; linked to Latin flumen, the word for the flowing water itself.
The Left Bank of the Seine in Paris; rive comes from the same Latin word as [[river]].
From Latin lacus, 'basin' or 'reservoir': named for the space that holds the water, not the water itself.
A Germanic, Old English word related to [[pound]] as in [[impound]]: the enclosure the water lives in.
Properly an enclosed body of water, unlike the [[ocean]]; the British favour 'sea', Americans 'ocean', and German See can mean lake.
From Latin oceanus, from Greek okeanos: in early Greek cosmology, the river circling the flat world and the god embodying it.
From an ancient root meaning left: if you face the rising sun in the east, north is on your left.
Shares a root with [[sun]], because in the northern hemisphere the sun is always to the south.
From a root meaning to become light, where the sun rises; related to Sanskrit ushas 'dawn', [[aurora]] and [[australis]]; unusual beside Germanic ost-forms.
Latin for southern, as in [[Austria]] and [[Australia]], yet related to [[east]]; the Romans may have misjudged which way Italy points.
From an ancient root meaning evening, where the sun sets; a cognate of Latin [[vesper]], not borrowed from it.
Irish and Scottish Gaelic for westward, also meaning behind you, because people oriented themselves facing the sunrise.
French for north, borrowed from English [[north]] and passed on to Spanish, even though Latin had its own compass words.
French for south, borrowed from English [[south]] and passed on to Spanish, a rare case of a basic word going from English to French.
French for east, borrowed from English [[east]], like the other French compass points, and then into Spanish.
French for west, borrowed from English [[west]], like the other French compass points, and then into Spanish.
The classical Latin for north, meaning 'seven ploughs': Ursa Major, called the Plough or Big Dipper, which points to the North Star.
Means with bears, after the constellation; covered in an earlier episode, and fittingly polar bears live there, unlike the [[Antarctic]].
Means without bears, the opposite of [[Arctic]]; fittingly, the South Pole has no polar bears.
From the Latin for east, the counterpart of [[occident]].
From the Latin for west, the counterpart of [[orient]].
Literally not knowing which way east is, from [[orient]]; Rob says it means 'to un-east yourself' and finds Americans prefer it.
The British form; per Rob it means undoing an orientation you had, a tiny difference from [[disorient]]; it's built on [[orientate]].
A back-formation from orientation, with [[orient]] later back-formed again as a verb; back-formations are often seen as lesser words.
